White sardinella (Sardinella albella) is a small, pelagic clupeid widely distributed across the Indo-West Pacific, where it supports important coastal fisheries. Field surveys indicate that the maximum recorded length for this species is 14 centimeters [Li = 14 centimeters], an ultimate total length that places it among the smaller members of the genus. In contrast, the total length at which puberty occurs, marking the onset of reproductive capability, has been estimated at 9 centimeters [Lp = 9 centimeters]. Growth studies based on length-frequency data suggest that individuals attain this size relatively quickly, reflecting a life history strategy that prioritizes early maturation in productive tropical waters. The maximum longevity of White sardinella, determined from otolith readings of wild-caught specimens, reaches approximately 2920 days [am = approximately 2920 days] when maintained at a stable water temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], a duration that is consistent with other short-lived, fast-growing clupeids from the same region that experience high natural mortality and compensate with rapid somatic growth and high reproductive output.

The early life stages of White sardinella are tightly coupled to local thermal conditions, with development proceeding rapidly in warm coastal waters. Egg hatching, or eclosion, occurs after an incubation period of just 3 days [ab = 3 days] at a water temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], a brief embryonic duration that is typical of small-bodied tropical clupeids whose transparent, pelagic eggs are incubated under warm, stable thermal regimes. The wet weight at birth, measured immediately following chorion rupture, is approximately 0.00032 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00032 grams], a value that corresponds closely to the predicted mass derived from the egg diameter range of 1 to 4 millimeters. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae are lecithotrophic and remain entirely dependent on endogenous reserves during the first few days post-hatching. The transition to exogenous feeding, marked by mouth opening and first prey capture, follows shortly after yolk absorption is completed, a critical period that determines early survival and recruitment success in the planktonic environment.

Reproductive output in White sardinella is seasonally concentrated and strongly influenced by ambient temperature. At 19 °C [T = 19 °C], the maximum rate of reproduction is expressed as females producing approximately 329 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 329 eggs per day], a value that is derived from the product of fecundity per spawning event and spawning frequency. Field studies indicate that a single gravid female can release a substantial number of oocytes during each spawning event, contributing to the species' high annual reproductive potential. This daily egg production rate, achieved under optimal thermal conditions, underpins the rapid population turnover characteristic of this short-lived, iteroparous species. The age at first reproduction, or first spawning event, has been documented at roughly 365 days after hatching [tR = roughly 365 days after hatching] when individuals are reared at 19 °C [T = 19 °C], a schedule that aligns with the attainment of the 9 centimeter length threshold at puberty. This relatively early age at first reproduction is a key component of the species' compensatory life history strategy, allowing it to maintain population stability despite high rates of natural mortality.

Adult body mass in White sardinella shows a strong allometric relationship with length, following a power-law growth trajectory typical of clupeiform fishes. The ultimate wet weight, representing the maximum body mass attained by fully grown adults, is estimated at 28.4 grams [Wwi = 28.4 grams], a value derived from the length-weight relationship using the asymptotic length of 14 centimeters. This moderate adult mass, roughly equivalent to two-thirds the mass of a standard table egg, reflects the slender, streamlined body plan of this coastal planktivore. Growth in weight decelerates markedly after sexual maturation, with most of the energetic surplus being diverted toward reproductive effort rather than continued somatic expansion. The wet weight at birth, at just 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams], underscores the enormous disparity in scale between the earliest larval stage and the fully grown adult, representing a mass increase of nearly five orders of magnitude. Achieving this growth trajectory requires sustained access to dense patches of zooplankton throughout the larval and juvenile phases, particularly in shallow, nutrient-rich coastal zones.

Comparative analyses with other sardinella species reveal that White sardinella occupies a distinct position along the fast-slow life history continuum. Its maximum life span of approximately 2920 days [am = approximately 2920 days] at 19 °C [T = 19 °C] places it notably below Sardinella longiceps, which can exceed a decade in cooler upwelling zones, highlighting an r-selected strategy where high fecundity and early maturation compensate for elevated adult mortality. The total length at which puberty is initiated, 9 centimeters [Lp = 9 centimeters], corresponds to approximately 64 percent of the ultimate total length of 14 centimeters [Li = 14 centimeters], a proportional size at onset that is typical for small clupeids. At 19 °C [T = 19 °C], the age at first reproduction of roughly 365 days after hatching [tR = roughly 365 days after hatching] coincides with a seasonal peak in planktonic productivity, ensuring that larvae emerge during periods of abundant food availability. This synchronization of reproductive timing with environmental conditions, combined with a rapid life cycle completed in under a decade, makes White sardinella particularly well-suited to variable tropical marine ecosystems.
